tidbits.text: "Which means" is where describing turns into explaining. Everything after it is your thinking, not the author's.
In 1793, Robespierre stood before France's National Convention, claimed to speak for the general will, and used that claim to justify executions. You'll read that speech in Casefile B.
Rousseau's general will can protect the common good, or it can be turned into a weapon against anyone who disagrees. A 5 explains both.
Rousseau and Montesquieu feared the same thing from opposite sides: Montesquieu feared one person holding all the power, and the general will can be used to justify exactly that.

exemplars.text: Rousseau says the general will looks at the common interest, which means a community should do what's good for everyone, not just what most people want.

Rousseau separates the general will, the common interest, from the will of all, a sum of private wants, which means a majority can be wrong. It also means the idea can be turned around: a leader who claims to speak for the general will can call anyone who disagrees an enemy, which is what Robespierre did in 1793.
exemplars.what_changed: The 4 explains one step. The 5 explains the idea, then explains its danger, so the reader sees why it matters in both directions.

techniques.explanation: Say what could go wrong with an idea, not just what it promises.
